"Firefighting operations are continuing but the situation continues to ease up," the Düren district administration said on Sunday. It said around two-thirds of Gey residents, who number around 1,800, had returned by Sunday morning after being given the all-clear on Saturday evening. The blaze, which has burnt out some 300 hectares (741 acres) has been described as the most serious wildfire in the recorded history of the western state of North Rhine-Westphalia. It has, however, now been dwarfed a nearby fire in Belgium's High Fens region , which is raging across 3,000 hectares and has approached to within 3 kilometers (2 miles) of the German border. The fires in western and other parts of Europe come amid a prolonged period without meaningful rain that has left undergrowth and many trees parched and highly inflammable. The case centers on a question asked by the journalist to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy earlier this month. The reporter asked Zelenskyy at a press conference in Belgrade what Europeans could do to help Ukraine kill more Russian soldiers as it fights Moscow's full-scale invasion . According to TASS, the journalist could face up to six years in a penal colony if convicted in Russia. Russian courts also hand down sentences in absentia. The journalist concerned covers southeastern Europe for the newspaper from Vienna. https://p.dw.com/p/5IuWb Skip next section Yiddish festival in Weimar draws thousands of visitors 08/16/2026 August 16, 2026 Yiddish festival in Weimar draws thousands of visitors Ahead of the festival, Weimar saw numerous events associated with Yiddish culture Image: Shendl Copitman/Religion News Service/AP Photo/picture alliance The 26th edition of a festival celebrating Yiddish and related cultures in the eastern city of Weimar ended on Saturday evening after some 12,000 people attended. This year, the focus was on women in Yiddish culture. Organizers said more than 300 people from around the world participated in workshops on the Yiddish language, music and dance, as well as youth projects. Participants could take part in dance courses Image: Shendl Copitman/Religion News Service/AP Photo/picture alliance "From the beginning, (the idea was) to present Yiddish culture as something which is alive, and not something that was entirely destroyed by the Shoah (Holocaust)," said Alan Bern, the founder and artistic director at Yiddish Summer Weimar, the body behind the festival. The Yiddish language first emerged in the Middle Ages in the German-speaking regions of Europe and later spread to other parts of Europe in various waves of Jewish migration. It is a Germanic language and partially mutually intelligible with German. In its written form it typically uses a modified form of the Hebrew alphabet. Who speaks Yiddish? In the 1930s, Yiddish was spoken as a vernacular by around 11 million Central and Eastern European Jews. The number of speakers was drastically diminished by the murder of some 6 million Jews in the Holocaust under Nazi Germany. Yiddish also declined as Jewish communities began adopting other languages like English, Hebrew, Russian and French. Now, the language is spoken by between 500,000 and 1 million people. It is mostly spoken as a mother tongue by certain tight-knit ultra-Orthodox communities in North America, Israel and to a lesser extent parts of western Europe. However, enthusiasts from other communities also learn it as a second language out of cultural or academic interest or in an effort to preserve it. Yiddish Summer Weimar presented 97 events in all this year in Weimar, Erfurt, Eisenach and other towns and municipalities in the eastern state of Thuringia, as well as in Istanbul, Agios Lavrentios in Greece and the German town of Zittau. https://p.dw.com/p/5IuE0 Skip next section German investment in US falls to three-year low 08/16/2026 August 16, 2026 German investment in US falls to three-year low German companies have cut investment in the United States to its lowest level in three years, as uncertainty over the Trump administration's trade policies weighs on new spending. Direct investment fell by almost two-thirds year on year to €4.3 billion ($5 billion) in the first half of 2026, according to calculations by the German Economic Institute, or IW, based on Bundesbank data. Compared with the first half of 2024, investment was down by nearly 80%. In the five years before the COVID-19 pandemic, German companies invested an average of €15.8 billion in the US during the first half of each year — almost four times the 2026 level. The IW said the decline continued a trend visible since Donald Trump began his second term in January 2025. Trump has repeatedly used or threatened import tariffs against US trading partners in an effort to secure concessions. The European Union last year struck a deal aimed at avoiding heavier US duties that included a pledge of $600 billion in investment. The IW said uncertainty around such policies was making German companies more reluctant to commit fresh capital in the US. In the first half of 2026, 23.2% of 8,320 reviews ended with protection being revoked or withdrawn, according to a government response to a parliamentary question from the socialist Left Party . The proportion has risen significantly from previous years. In 2025, only 3.7% of reviewed Syrian cases resulted in protection being withdrawn, compared with 3.1% in 2024. Most cases involved the loss of formal refugee status or subsidiary protection — a separate status accorded to refugees but with fewer protections. Syrians who lose protection may still qualify for another residence permit, for example through employment, or potentially for German citizenship. Even without another legal status, deportation to Syria remains difficult because returns require cooperation from Syrian authorities. What is Germany's debate around Syrian refugee returns? Germany resumed deportations to Syria following Assad's fall in December 2024. They were the first deportations since 2011, when Syria's civil war broke out. Earlier this year, Chancellor Friedrich Merz suggested that some 80% of Syrians living in Germany could return to Syria over the next three years. The comments sparked considerable political backlash, with experts arguing the timeframe was unrealistic and others pointing to the large number of Syrians working in Germany's already understaffed medical system . Around 973,000 Syrians were living in Germany at the end of 2023, with some 700,000 having refugee status or subsidiary protection. Over 200,000 Syrians have acquired German citizenship — making them the largest group of new naturalizations in recent years — and around 70,000 have permanent residence. https://p.dw.com/p/5Iu3E Skip next section Welcome back! 08/16/2026 August 16, 2026 Welcome back! By David Dalton, 30 July 2026, https://www.nucnet.org/news/uk-needs-urgent-guidance-on-preferred-reactor-concepts-says-fission-materials-roadmap-7-4-2026 Interim report lays out priorities on shaping next generation of nuclear plants The UK urgently needs guidance on preferred reactor concepts and operating environments so it can prioritise materials research as it strives to shape the next generation of nuclear reactors which will power the country’s nuclear future, a report has said. The UK Fission Materials Roadmap Interim Report, published by the United Kingdom National Nuclear Laboratory (UKNNL) and the Henry Royce Institute, said a decision is needed within one to two years on whether the UK should build a domestic materials test reactor. Within five years the government needs to establish a national materials archive to preserve irreplaceable irradiated material samples The report also called for long-term funding commitments of at least five years to support sustained research programmes. Four major technical themes are set out in the report: structural materials, fuels and cladding, disposability of materials and irradiation damage. These sit alongside six separate priorities: skills, infrastructure, funding, qualification, modelling and policy. Together, they form the foundation of a full roadmap planned for publication in late 2026. Gareth Headdock, chief science and technology officer and deputy chief executive officer of UKNNL, said the interim report is the product of genuine collaboration across the UK nuclear sector. “From structural steels to advanced fuels and waste disposability, we have identified the priorities that matter most and the decisions that cannot wait. “The decisions ahead – on reactor concepts, materials test infrastructure and long-term funding – are consequential ones, and it is vital that we get them right.” David Knowles, chief executive officer of the Henry Royce Institute, the UK’s national institute for advanced materials research and innovation, said the momentum behind the UK nuclear sector is clear. He said recent agreements between Rolls-Royce SMR, UKNNL and the Japan Atomic Energy Agency to accelerate the deployment of advanced nuclear technologies demonstrate the growing international confidence in UK nuclear capability. “At the same time, the continued progress of Rolls-Royce SMR in securing commercial opportunities and advancing deployment highlights the strength of UK nuclear engineering and the scale of the opportunity ahead,” he said. Rolls-Royce SMR, a subsidiary of blue chip engineering giant Rolls-Royce, and Czech state power company ČEZ are working on plans to deploy up to 3 GW of SMR capacity in the Czech Republic. The company, a Rolls-Royce subsidiary, is also deploying three units in the UK with the potential for six, with a launch programme of three units in Sweden . REUTERS/Stringer Russia and Ukraine Press on With Energy Strikes Despite Trump Reuters Total Views: 651 September 15, 2026 KYIV, Sept 15 (Reuters) – Russia hit petrol stations in Kyiv on Tuesday and Ukraine struck a Russian oil refinery, as the warring sides carried on with strikes on each other’s energy targets despite an announcement by U.S. President Donald Trump that they had agreed to stop. Russia launched 200 drones at Ukraine’s capital and other cities in overnight attacks, killing two people. In addition to petrol stations in Kyiv it struck energy and port infrastructure in other regions, Ukrainian officials said. For its part, Ukraine hit a Russian oil refinery in Syzran in Russia’s Samara region on the Volga River, and also drone production facilities in the Taganrog and Oryol regions, President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said. The Samara governor said an industrial facility was hit there without identifying it. The Taganrog governor said a warehouse of e-commerce firm Ozon was struck there. “Russia continues to attack our energy sector, regular logistics and critical infrastructure. And our responses to them for this are tangible,” Zelenskiy said on the Telegram app. Trump said on Monday that Ukraine and Russia had agreed to halt strikes on each other’s energy infrastructure, which he says are the main factor in a global fuel shortage that has driven diesel prices in the United States to record highs. Zelenskiy said that Ukraine was ready to halt such strikes but required credible guarantees from its partners that Russia would also stop. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Trump’s suggestion was a “very good idea”, but that it would take more to bring down global fuel prices. “It is necessary to ensure safe commercial shipping and navigation here, including for oil tankers,” Peskov said, adding that Russia would stay in touch with the U.S. about Trump’s proposal. Russia has been targeting Ukrainian energy infrastructure with missiles and drones persistently since Moscow launched its full-scale invasion in 2022, and began targeting petrol stations in Kyiv and other cities in recent weeks. Kyiv has stepped up long-range attacks on Russia this year, including a campaign targeting oil refineries that has caused fuel shortages. Previous attempts by the U.S. administration to broker a ceasefire on energy infrastructure have failed. EXPLOSIONS ROCK KYIV Ukrainian officials said that one person was killed in Russian attacks on Kyiv and another died in the city of Zaporizhzhia in the southeast of the country. Two petrol stations in Kyiv were damaged, the state energy company Naftogaz said. Reuters heard several explosions in Kyiv and the surrounding region. So far this year, Russia has damaged 16 petrol stations in Kyiv, city officials said, adding that there was no risk of fuel shortages due to diversified logistics. “We see that the enemy started to strike petrol stations in Kyiv with precision,” Andrii Tkachov from Kyiv’s military administration told Ukrainian TV. As Moscow’s attack on Ukraine was under way, neighboring Poland held military aviation operations as a preventive step, Poland’s Armed Forces said, adding later that there was no violation of its airspace. In Lithuania, a NATO fighter jet shot down a drone early on Tuesday, the National Crisis Management Centre said. It did not say the origin of the drone. Similar incidents in the Baltic region in recent months have involved Ukrainian drones that Kyiv says were steered across NATO borders by Russian signal jamming. (Reporting by Olena Harmash in Kyiv, Anna Pruchnicka in Gdansk, Jekaterina Golubkova in Tokyo; Editing by Peter Graff) (c) Copyright Thomson Reuters 2026. https://www.politico.eu/article/ukraine-.text: Ukraine struck an oil terminal in St. Petersburg Sunday morning in what Russian state media called “one of the biggest drone attacks of the year.” Alexander Beglov, governor of St. Petersburg, said on Telegram Sunday that the city underwent a “massive” overnight attack from Ukrainian drones. “The Ministry of Emergency Situations continues to extinguish fires at the Petersburg Oil Terminal, the Ruchyi oil depot, and industrial warehouses in the Kolpino district,” he said, adding that one person died and several others were injured in the incident. The drone strikes come as Kyiv and Moscow ramp up attacks on each other’s infrastructure. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said last week he had ordered the resumption of strikes on Russian oil refineries following a three-day pause after U.S. President Donald Trump declared he had brokered an energy ceasefire between Ukraine and Russia. Advertisement Advertisement Trump repeatedly urged Ukraine to halt its attacks and blamed the country for rising fuel prices — while also calling for Zelenskyy to be replaced as president . Writing on X Sunday morning, the Ukrainian president highlighted Moscow’s continued attacks on Ukraine. “In total, over this past week, the Russians have attacked Ukraine with almost 2,700 attack drones, 1,700 aerial bombs, and 66 missiles, most of them ballistic,” he wrote, adding that the U.S. “should see that Russia is not taking any reciprocal steps in response to sanctions relief or agreements.” Separately, Vilnius said that a suspected drone may have self-detonated in Lithuania while on a flight path toward Latvia Sunday morning. A spokesperson for the Lithuanian armed forces said NATO air defense mission fighter jets were scrambled in response to the incident near the Latvian border. The provenance of the suspected drone is unclear, but Robertas ​Kaunas, Lithuania’s defense minister, said the object was likely a ​drone which had entered the country from Poland, adding that he had proposed a ⁠joint investigation with his Polish counterpart. Police searches are also underway in eastern Poland after reports of an unidentified object entering the country’s airspace following a Russian attack on Ukraine.
